title: Bind an Artifact to Its Source
concept: Verify release identity and digest metadata

writing.summary: Verify release identity and digest metadata.
writing.rule: A filename or version label does not prove which bytes were tested.
writing.explanation:
A release artifact should have an identity that can be compared with the tested source and the expected content digest. Reusing a mutable latest filename makes rollback and incident investigation harder. Retain the source revision, exact target, digest and verification receipt beside immutable artifact bytes.

The lab validates metadata: a full lowercase 40-hex Git object ID, a lowercase 64-hex SHA-256 digest and an exact match with an independently supplied expected digest. It does not calculate SHA-256 or prove the claim by validating string shape. The actual delivery script computes the digest from built bytes with a standard tool, then compares it before promotion. A digest detects changed bytes when the expected digest is trusted; it is not an author signature. Keep signing and provenance decisions explicit rather than calling a checksum an authenticity guarantee.

The route project is Task Ledger: first keep a reproducible source history, then expose its data through a CLI and HTTP boundary, persist it in SQL, diagnose failures and prepare a release. This lesson owns one contract in that project. Run the worked example before changing the starter and explain which input makes the tempting shortcut fail.

Terminal practice: Run the desktop delivery script, inspect its source revision and computed artifact SHA-256, then modify an artifact copy and observe verification fail.

The compiler lab is independent of the reading question. Edit solution.rs; the app supplies a separate caller with normal, empty and adversarial inputs. A successful unchanged demonstration does not prove your implementation. After the lab, apply the same contract to the route companion project. Its README separates the on-device adapter from the desktop Cargo/TCP profile.

writing.task: Validate lowercase hexadecimal commit(40) and digest/expected(64), then require digest==expected. This checks metadata only; actual digest computation belongs to the supplied build-byte verification step. Keep the public signature. Open the compiler lab and edit solution.rs; do not edit the private verification caller.
writing.success: The separate caller accepts the changed solution and rejects unchanged TODO, a wrong implementation and a printed success message.
writing.question: Does a well-formed SHA-256 string prove the artifact bytes match?
answers: No, compute and compare the actual bytes against a trusted expected digest
A checksum automatically identifies the publisher
writing.feedback: String shape, byte integrity and publisher authenticity are different properties.

recall.question: Why does `artifact_matches("main", digest, digest)` return false, and why does the policy insist on a full commit ID?
recall.answer: `main` is a moving branch name, not a 40-character lowercase hex object ID. Only a full commit identity binds the artifact to the exact source that was tested, which rollback and incident investigation depend on.

recall.question: The SHA-256 digest computed from the built bytes matches the expected digest. What does that prove, and what does it not?
recall.answer: If the expected digest is trusted, it proves the bytes have not changed since that digest was recorded. It is not an author signature: authenticity and provenance need separate signing decisions.
